name: Galileo Galilei
info: Galileo Galilei, an Italian astronomer, physicist and engineer of Pisa, Padua and Florence, whose telescope observations and studies of motion helped found modern science and whose defence of heliocentrism led to his condemnation by the Inquisition in 1633.

facts.born: 15 February 1564, in Pisa, then part of the Duchy of Florence; first of six children of the lutenist and music theorist Vincenzo Galilei and Giulia Ammannati
facts.died: 8 January 1642, at Arcetri near Florence, aged 77, after a fever and heart palpitations, still under house arrest
facts.role: Instructor at the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno in Florence (1588); chair of mathematics at Pisa (1589); professor at the University of Padua (1592–1610); philosopher and chief mathematician to the Grand Duke of Tuscany
facts.known: the improved telescope and the Starry Messenger (1610); Jupiter's four largest moons and the phases of Venus; the laws of falling bodies and inertia; the principle of relativity; the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632); his trial by the Inquisition; Two New Sciences (1638)

t: With telescopes he built himself, Galileo saw the Moon's mountains, Jupiter's four largest moons and the phases of Venus, observations that made the Ptolemaic model untenable.
He joined experiment and mathematics in the study of motion, describing uniform acceleration in falling bodies, inertia and the principle of relativity that later underlay Newton's laws.
His defence of Copernican heliocentrism brought an order to abandon it in 1616 and, after his Dialogue of 1632, a sentence as 'vehemently suspect of heresy' and house arrest for the rest of his life.
dyk: The word 'telescope' was coined for Galileo's instrument at a banquet in 1611, when he was made a member of Prince Federico Cesi's Accademia dei Lincei; a fellow member coined 'microscope' for another of his instruments a few years later.
ev: Galileo is appointed to the chair of mathematics at Pisa, moving to the University of Padua in 1592
Galileo publishes the Starry Messenger, reporting his telescope observations, including four moons of Jupiter
Cardinal Bellarmine orders Galileo to abandon the opinion that the Earth moves around the Sun
Galileo publishes The Assayer, dedicated to the new pope, Urban VIII
Galileo publishes the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems
The Inquisition finds Galileo 'vehemently suspect of heresy' and he is forced to recant
Two New Sciences is published in Holland, and Galileo goes completely blind

sections.early:
Galileo was born in Pisa, then part of the Duchy of Florence, on 15 February 1564, into an ancient noble family. He was the first of six children of Vincenzo Galilei, a leading lutenist, composer and music theorist and a member of the Florentine Camerata, and Giulia Ammannati, the daughter of a prominent merchant. Galileo became an accomplished lutenist himself. His father's experiments on stretched strings, which related pitch to tension, gave the boy an early example of mathematics applied to physical things.

When he was eight the family moved to Florence, leaving him in the care of Muzio Tedaldi for two years; at ten he joined them and studied under Jacopo Borghini, then, from 1575 to 1578, at the Vallombrosa Abbey, mainly in logic. He seriously considered the priesthood, but at his father's urging he enrolled at the University of Pisa in 1580 to study medicine, the better-paid profession. After chancing on a lecture on geometry, he persuaded his reluctant father to let him study mathematics and natural philosophy instead.

His family later weighed on him. After his father died in 1591 he was responsible for his younger brother Michelagnolo, who could not pay his share of their sisters' dowries, and these burdens may have pushed Galileo towards inventions that would bring in money.
sections.rise:
As a student in 1581 Galileo noticed that a swinging chandelier seemed to keep the same time whatever the width of its swing, and he tested the idea with two pendulums. He built a thermoscope and in 1586 published a small book on a hydrostatic balance he had invented, which first drew scholars' attention to him. In 1588 he taught perspective and chiaroscuro at the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno in Florence and lectured on the shape and size of Dante's Inferno.

He was appointed to the chair of mathematics at Pisa in 1589 and in 1592 moved to the University of Padua, where he taught geometry, mechanics and astronomy until 1610. There he obtained a Venetian patent for a horse-powered water pump in 1594 and between 1595 and 1598 devised a geometric and military compass for gunners and surveyors, of which more than 100 were made and sold. He observed Kepler's Supernova in 1604 and argued that such new stars were distant, against the Aristotelian belief that the heavens never change.

In 1609, perhaps working only from descriptions of the Dutch telescope, he built one of about 3× magnification and later versions of up to about 30×, and showed an early instrument to Venetian lawmakers on 25 August 1609. Telescopes also became a profitable sideline, sold to merchants, and he named the moons he found the Medicean stars in honour of his future patron, Cosimo II de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany.
sections.deeds:
From late 1609 Galileo turned his telescope on the sky. He deduced that the uneven light on the Moon came from mountains and craters and estimated their heights. On 7 January 1610 he saw three small 'fixed stars' near Jupiter and by 15 January concluded that four bodies were orbiting it; Simon Marius found them independently, and they bear the names Marius gave them. He published these findings in the Sidereus Nuncius in March 1610. From September 1610 he saw that Venus shows a full set of phases, which made the Ptolemaic model untenable. He also found the Milky Way to be a mass of stars, studied sunspots and recorded Neptune in 1612 without recognising it as a planet.

His second achievement was in the science of motion, which he studied by joining experiment and mathematics. He held that a falling body accelerates uniformly when resistance is negligible, that the distance travelled from rest is proportional to the square of the time, that a projectile's ideal path is a parabola, and that a body keeps its velocity unless impeded. In the Dialogue he set out the principle that the laws of physics are the same in any system moving at constant speed in a straight line. He wrote in The Assayer (1623) that the book of the universe 'is written in the language of mathematics'.

He also built an early compound microscope, used by 1624, proposed using the moons of Jupiter to find longitude, and late in life designed an escapement for a pendulum clock.
sections.opponents:
Not all of Galileo's science stood. His theory of the tides, which he offered as physical proof that the Earth moves, predicted one high tide a day and failed to explain the observed tides, and he dismissed the idea, held by Johannes Kepler, that the Moon causes them. His conjectures on comets in the dispute with the Jesuit Orazio Grassi are now known to be mistaken. The story of balls dropped from the Leaning Tower of Pisa, told by his pupil Vincenzo Viviani, is generally held by historians to have been at most a thought experiment, with Stillman Drake an exception. His disputes, including a long and bitter feud with Christoph Scheiner over sunspots, alienated many Jesuits.

The great conflict was with the Church. In 1615 Father Niccolò Lorini denounced his letter to Benedetto Castelli, which argued that the Bible was an authority on faith and morals rather than science. In February 1616 an Inquisitorial commission declared heliocentrism 'formally heretical', and Cardinal Bellarmine ordered Galileo not to hold, teach or defend it. Pope Urban VIII later asked him to present both sides; in the Dialogue of 1632 the Aristotelian Simplicio often seemed a fool, and the Pope took it as disrespect. Most historians agree Galileo had not intended satire. Dava Sobel argues that Urban, under political pressure, felt betrayed.

At his trial in 1633 Galileo maintained, rather implausibly, that he had not held Copernican views after 1616, even under the threat of torture.
sections.last:
The sentence of 22 June 1633 found Galileo 'vehemently suspect of heresy', required him to 'abjure, curse and detest' the opinion that the Sun stands still at the centre and the Earth moves, banned the Dialogue and, without announcement at the trial, forbade the publication of any of his works. His imprisonment was commuted the next day to house arrest, which lasted the rest of his life. The legend that he muttered 'And yet it moves' is first known in writing a century after his death.

After a stay with Ascanio Piccolomini, Archbishop of Siena, he returned in 1634 to his villa at Arcetri near Florence. He was ordered to read the Seven Penitential Psalms weekly for three years, a duty his daughter Maria Celeste, a nun at the convent of San Matteo, took on herself with Church permission; she died on 2 April 1634. Galileo had fathered three children out of wedlock with Marina Gamba; his two daughters became nuns, and his son Vincenzo was legitimised as his heir.

Under arrest he wrote Two New Sciences, on kinematics and the strength of materials, published in Holland in 1638 to avoid Catholic censorship. That year he went completely blind. He kept receiving visitors, who brought him new scientific books, until his death on 8 January 1642, aged 77. Urban VIII and Cardinal Francesco Barberini blocked the Grand Duke's plan for a tomb in the main body of Santa Croce; he was reburied there in 1737.
sections.legacy:
Galileo has been called the father of observational astronomy, classical physics, the scientific method and modern science. His work on motion, with the largely independent work of Kepler and René Descartes, prepared the classical mechanics of Isaac Newton, and his principle of relativity is central to Einstein's special theory of relativity. Albert Einstein called him the father of modern physics, and Stephen Hawking said he probably bore more responsibility for the birth of modern science than anyone else. Steven Weinberg notes that he wrote the Dialogue in Italian, with little mathematics, so any literate Italian could read it.

The Church's ban eased slowly. Reprinting of his works was allowed in 1718, Pope Benedict XIV authorised a complete edition with a mildly censored Dialogue in 1741, the general prohibition on heliocentric works was lifted in 1758, and the Dialogue left the Index in 1835. In the 19th century Protestant polemicists used the affair to attack Catholicism. In 1990 Cardinal Ratzinger quoted the philosopher Paul Feyerabend's view that the verdict had been 'rational and just' without clearly saying whether he agreed. On 31 October 1992 Pope John Paul II acknowledged that the Inquisition had erred in condemning him.

The four large moons of Jupiter are called the Galilean moons, and the Galileo spacecraft bears his name. Bertolt Brecht's play Life of Galileo (1938) told his story, and 2009, four centuries after his first telescope observations, was the International Year of Astronomy.

summary: Galileo Galilei of Pisa built improved telescopes, discovered Jupiter's largest moons and the phases of Venus, and joined experiment and mathematics in a new science of motion. His defence of heliocentrism led to his condemnation by the Inquisition in 1633 and house arrest until his death in 1642; the Church acknowledged its error in 1992.
